verdict.reasoning: Patient reports onset 'about two to three days ago' and describes 'short of breath... I'm just wheezing a bit and coughing.'

She says, 'about two to three days ago I was running with a friend... but I found myself actually short of breath. I'm not really short of breath when I'm walking, but definitely if I'm walking briskly now.'

She first says she uses the blue inhaler 'as and when I have symptoms' and then adds 'Yeah, and morning and evening to kind of prevent it as well.' This indicates both PRN and prophylactic use, not strictly daily scheduled use; the fact omits the 'as and when' usage and overstates it as purely daily morning and evening.
She states, 'I've used my blue inhaler, but to no avail. It hasn't really helped me.'
When asked about phlegm, she replies, 'No, I don't. I'm not coughing up much sputum,' consistent with a largely dry cough.
Asthma is referenced repeatedly: 'Have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?' and 'When was the last time you had an asthma attack?' indicating a history of asthma.
In response to 'Have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?' she answers, 'No, I haven't.'
To 'When was the last time you had an asthma attack?' she replies, 'About three to four years ago.'
To 'When was the last time you had an asthma review with our nurse?' she replies, 'About two years ago.'
She lists 'salbutamol' among her medications: 'My history is salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well.'
She confirms daily and twice-daily use of Clenil (clinol): 'I think I'm using that every day.' and to 'Is it twice a day?' she answers, 'Yes.'
Cetraben is listed: 'My history is salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well.'
'Hydrocortisone' is included in her current medications: 'salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I'm taking as well.'
When asked about allergies, she says, 'I have hay fever... Sorry, I have hay fever.'
She states, 'My brother's asthmatic.'
She states, 'My sister has eczema.'
After some clarification, clinician says, 'Okay. Let's say it's about 380. Yeah, yeah. Three. Okay. Right, so that's your normal.' indicating a normal peak flow around 380 L/min.
Clinician states, 'it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation,' referring to her asthma, supporting assessment of asthma exacerbation.

Symptoms described are 'short of breath... I'm just wheezing a bit and coughing,' and she says the blue inhaler has been 'to no avail. It hasn't really helped me,' indicating an exacerbation with increased SOB, wheeze, cough, and ineffective current inhaler use.
Clinician advises, 'I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days.'
Instruction given: 'you can use your blue inhaler as and when. Okay. Use it maximum about every two to four hours.'
Clinician advises, 'If you're using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day,' referring to the brown (Clenil) inhaler.

She is told, 'if you're using the asthma, you know, the blue inhalers every two to four hours. And your breathing's getting really worse. Then you would need to take yourself to A. E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment.'
Future GP actions described: 'we're going to examine your chest. Yeah. Make you do the peak reading. So depending on what we find, you might need some antibiotics or some steroids.'
Follow-up plan is, 'I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days' and 'Book an appointment... to see... I will recommend that you need a face to face.'
